los.text: Describe the clinical signs and symptoms, likely diagnosis, investigations and treatment following upper arm/shoulder trauma
los.html:
InjuryMechanism / featuresIx & treatment
Anterior shoulder dislocation (95%)Fall on outstretched/abducted, externally rotated arm. Squared-off shoulder, arm held in slight abduction
  • X-ray (AP + axillary/Y view) before and after reduction.
  • Check axillary nerve (regimental badge sensation, deltoid).
  • Closed reduction under analgesia/sedation, sling
Posterior dislocationSeizures, electric shock. Arm internally rotated; "light bulb" sign on APEasily missed; reduce
Proximal humerus fractureElderly, osteoporotic, FOOSHX-ray; most treated in collar and cuff + early physio; displaced → ORIF/arthroplasty
Humeral shaft fractureDirect blow/twistCheck radial nerve (wrist drop, sensory loss over first dorsal web space). Functional brace
Clavicle fractureFall on shoulder; middle thirdSling; surgery if open, skin tenting, NV compromise
Rotator cuff tear>40, fall or degenerative; weak abduction/external rotationUSS/MRI; physio or repair
ACJ dislocationFall on point of shoulder; step deformitySling; surgery for high grades
  • Assessment: ATLS if high energy; inspect, palpate, ROM; neurovascular status before and after any manipulation; X-ray two views.
Always document axillary nerve function before and after reducing a shoulder dislocation.

los.text: Describe the structure and function of musculoskeletal connective tissues (bone, cartilage, ligaments, tendons)
los.html:
Bone
  • Osteoblasts (build; osteoid), osteocytes (mechanosensing, in lacunae, connected by canaliculi), osteoclasts (resorb; from monocyte lineage, RANKL-driven).
  • Matrix: type I collagen (tensile strength) + hydroxyapatite (compressive strength).
  • Cortical (Haversian osteons; 80% mass) vs trabecular/cancellous (metabolically active; vertebrae, metaphyses).
  • Functions: support, protection, movement, mineral store (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻), haematopoiesis.
Hyaline (articular) cartilage
  • Avascular, aneural
  • Chondrocytes in lacunae
  • Type II collagen + proteoglycans (aggrecan, hyaluronan) hold water → resists compression
  • Low friction.
  • Nutrition by diffusion from synovial fluid
  • Poor repair.
  • Zones: superficial (tangential), middle, deep, calcified.
Fibrocartilage(type I + II collagen)Menisci, IV discs, labrum, pubic symphysis.
  • Ligaments (bone→bone) and tendons (muscle→bone): dense regular connective tissue
  • Parallel type I collagen + fibroblasts (tenocytes)
  • Poor blood supply → slow healing.
  • Tendons transmit force
  • Ligaments stabilise joints and give proprioception.
  • Tendon–bone insertion = enthesis.

los.text: Describe the structural and physiological changes that occur in articular cartilage during common disease states and normal ageing
los.html:
Normal ageing
  • ↓ water content
  • ↓ proteoglycan size/aggregation
  • ↑ collagen cross-linking (advanced glycation end-products → yellowing, stiffness)
  • ↓ chondrocyte number and response to growth factors.
  • Cartilage thins but surface stays intact.
  • This is not the same as OA.
Osteoarthritis
  • Early ↑ water content and swelling, proteoglycan loss, collagen network breakdown (MMPs, ADAMTS aggrecanases driven by IL-1, TNF-α)
  • → fibrillation and fissuring
  • → full-thickness loss and eburnation of bone.
  • Chondrocytes cluster ("cloning").
  • Bone: subchondral sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes.
  • Synovium: low-grade inflammation.
Rheumatoid arthritisSynovial pannus invades cartilage and bone at the margins; cytokine-driven enzymatic destruction → periarticular erosions, uniform joint space loss.
Septic arthritisRapid cartilage destruction by bacterial and neutrophil enzymes (days).
Crystal arthropathiesUrate (gout) or CPPD (pseudogout, chondrocalcinosis) deposits damage cartilage.

los.text: Describe the main causes and different types of fracture, and explain the processes involved in fracture healing
los.html:
CausesTraumatic (high or low energy), pathological (weakened bone: osteoporosis, metastases, myeloma, Paget's, osteomalacia), stress/fatigue (repetitive loading: metatarsals, tibia in runners/military).
Description
  • Open vs closed
  • Site
  • Pattern (transverse = bending, oblique/spiral = twisting, comminuted = >2 fragments, high energy, avulsion, compression/impacted, greenstick/buckle in children, Salter–Harris physeal injuries)
  • Displacement, angulation, rotation, shortening.
Healing (secondary/indirect, with callus)
  • Haematoma and inflammation (days 1–7): clot, cytokines, macrophages, necrotic bone ends.
  • Soft callus (weeks 2–3): granulation tissue → fibrocartilage; fibroblasts, chondroblasts, angiogenesis.
  • Hard callus (weeks 3–12): endochondral ossification → woven bone.
  • Remodelling (months–years): woven → lamellar bone (Wolff's law).
Primary (direct) healingRigid fixation with anatomical reduction (compression plates) → cutting cones, no callus.
Impaired healingSmoking, diabetes, NSAIDs (debated), steroids, infection, poor blood supply (scaphoid, femoral neck, distal tibia), excessive movement, malnutrition → delayed union, non-union, malunion.

los.text: Describe the structure and main functions of the integumentary system
los.html:
Epidermis(keratinised stratified squamous; avascular)
  • Stratum basale (stem cells, melanocytes, Merkel cells)
  • → spinosum (Langerhans cells, desmosomes)
  • → granulosum (keratohyalin, lamellar bodies, barrier lipids)
  • → lucidum (thick skin only)
  • → corneum.
  • Turnover ~4 weeks.
Dermis
  • Papillary (loose; capillaries, Meissner corpuscles) and reticular (dense irregular collagen, elastin).
  • Contains vessels, nerves, hair follicles, sweat and sebaceous glands, Pacinian corpuscles.
HypodermisAdipose tissue (insulation, energy store, cushioning).
AppendagesHair, nails, eccrine sweat glands (thermoregulation; sympathetic cholinergic), apocrine glands (axilla, groin), sebaceous glands (sebum, holocrine).
Functions
  • Barrier (physical, chemical, microbial, UV via melanin)
  • Thermoregulation (sweat, vasodilation/constriction)
  • Sensation
  • Vitamin D synthesis (7-dehydrocholesterol + UVB)
  • Immune surveillance (Langerhans cells)
  • Water retention
  • Communication/appearance.

los.text: Describe the analgesic treatment of upper arm trauma
los.html:
Assess pain (scale), neurovascular status and contraindications. Immobilise (sling, splint): this is analgesic in itself. Ice and elevation.
WHO analgesic ladder(adapted for acute pain)
  • Paracetamol ± NSAID → weak opioid (codeine) → strong opioid (morphine).
  • In severe acute trauma go straight to IV morphine, titrated in small increments (e.g. 1–2 mg) with antiemetic and monitoring of RR/sedation.
Paracetamol1 g QDS (reduce if <50 kg or hepatic risk).
NSAIDs(ibuprofen, naproxen)Avoid in renal impairment, GI bleed/ulcer, asthma sensitivity, anticoagulation, late pregnancy, elderly; give PPI cover. Theoretical concern about fracture healing.
Entonox(50% N₂O/O₂)Short procedures; avoid with pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, head injury.
Regional anaesthesiae.g. interscalene or haematoma block; Bier's block for forearm.
Procedural sedation for dislocation reduction (e.g. midazolam, propofol, ketamine) with airway monitoring.
Opioid side effects: nausea, constipation, sedation, respiratory depression (reversal: naloxone).

los.text: Describe the fundamental principles of evidence-based practice
los.html:
EBP(Sackett)Using the current best evidence conscientiously and judiciously in decisions about individual patients.
Three componentsBest research evidence + clinical expertise + patient values and preferences.
5 steps (5 A's)
  • Ask (PICO question: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome)
  • → Acquire (search: Cochrane, PubMed, NICE)
  • → Appraise (validity, results, applicability)
  • → Apply
  • → Assess/audit outcomes.
Hierarchy of evidence
  • Systematic reviews/meta-analyses of RCTs > RCTs > cohort > case–control > case series/reports > expert opinion.
  • Quality matters more than design alone (GRADE).
Key statisticsRelative risk, absolute risk reduction, NNT = 1/ARR, sensitivity/specificity, confidence intervals, p-values.
LimitationsEvidence may not apply to your patient (multimorbidity, elderly excluded from trials); publication bias; industry funding; guidelines lag behind.
